name: GitHub
one_liner: No review: register an OAuth App (or GitHub App) in a few minutes and any GitHub user can connect at once; the only gate is per-organization approval when an org restricts third-party apps.
difficulty_reason: Self-serve registration with no app review, no user cap and no verification; the only friction is org owners who must approve your app before it can see their org's private data.
time_to_production: Same day (no provider review); add time per customer org for owner approval if OAuth app access restrictions are on

approval.required_for: Nothing for normal use. A review happens only if you choose to list the app on GitHub Marketplace. Separately, each organization with OAuth app access restrictions enabled must have an org owner approve your OAuth App before it can reach that org's private resources.
approval.who_reviews: No one for registration. GitHub Marketplace onboarding team if you list. Each customer org's owners for org access.
approval.typical_wait: No wait for registration. Marketplace review: not published ("An onboarding expert will reach out to you"). Org approval: depends on each org's owners.

account_prerequisites: Any GitHub personal account, or an organization where you have admin access (recommended so the app does not depend on one person)
Authorization callback URL on a domain you control (HTTPS recommended; loopback 127.0.0.1 allowed for native/desktop apps)
No business verification, verified domain or privacy policy is needed to register (a privacy policy link is required only for a Marketplace listing)

steps.title: Choose OAuth App or GitHub App
steps.detail: OAuth App: user authorizes, token acts as the user across everything they can access, scopes are coarse (repo grants all private repo data). GitHub App: fine-grained permissions, user picks repositories at install, can also act as itself, rate limits scale. GitHub recommends GitHub Apps. For an agent that should touch only chosen repos, prefer a GitHub App; for broad 'act as me' access, or enterprise-object access, an OAuth App is simpler. Composio's default GitHub auth config is OAuth2 with a client ID and secret, and works with either app type's credentials.

steps.title: Register the app
steps.detail: Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps > New OAuth App (or under an organization's settings). Fill Application name, Homepage URL, optional description, and Authorization callback URL. Up to 10 callback URLs are allowed. A user or org can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

steps.title: Set the callback URL
steps.detail: If you use Composio with your own app, add Composio's redirect URI shown in the auth config (default https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add). Leave wildcard matching off unless you control every subdomain and path.

steps.title: Decide on token expiry
steps.detail: 'Expire user access tokens' is checked by default for new OAuth apps (8 hour access token, 6 month refresh token). Keep it on only if your token store refreshes tokens; uncheck it otherwise. Composio stores and refreshes tokens for you.

steps.title: Generate a client secret
steps.detail: On the app page, generate a client secret and copy it once. Store client ID and secret in your secret manager.

steps.title: Wire up the flow
steps.detail: Web flow: GET https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize with client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state and PKCE (S256). Exchange the code (valid 10 minutes) at POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token. With Composio: create a custom GitHub auth config with client ID, secret and scopes, then pass its ID in auth_configs.

steps.title: Test with a personal account and an org account
steps.detail: Connect a personal account, then an account in an org with OAuth app access restrictions on, to see the 'request approval' path your users will hit.

steps.title: Tell customers how to approve your app for their org
steps.detail: Write a help-page section: org owner goes to Organization Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy, clicks Review next to your app, then Grant access.

steps.title: (Optional) List on GitHub Marketplace
steps.detail: Only if you want discovery or GitHub billing. Needs privacy policy, support link, logo, screenshots, webhooks for plan changes, and acceptance of the Marketplace Developer Agreement; then Request publish. Paid plans need a verified publisher org and 200 users (OAuth Apps) or 100 installations (GitHub Apps).

nuances: No user cap and no review for OAuth Apps or GitHub Apps used outside Marketplace.
OAuth Apps changed on 14 Aug 2026: up to 10 callback URLs, opt-in or default expiring tokens (8h access, 6 month refresh), and visible per-URL wildcard matching.
Apps that had a single callback URL before 3 Aug 2026 (all older OAuth apps) have wildcard matching enabled; disable it if you do not need it.
With wildcard matching off, redirect_uri must exactly match a registered callback URL. With it on, any subdomain or subpath of the callback matches, but host and port must match.
Loopback redirect (http://127.0.0.1/path) may use any port at runtime; GitHub follows the RFC advice to use 127.0.0.1, not localhost.
If redirect_uri is omitted, GitHub redirects to the first callback URL registered.
Authorization code expires after 10 minutes. Device flow codes expire after 15 minutes.

Refresh rotates both tokens: once used, the old refresh token and old access token stop working. Scopes cannot change on refresh. Store the new refresh token atomically to avoid races in concurrent agent workers.
Turning on expiry globally does not expire existing tokens; users must re-authorize to get expiring ones. Request offline_access to opt in per sign-in during rollout.
Limit of 10 tokens per user/application/scope combination; an 11th revokes an older one. Creating more than 10 tokens per hour triggers a re-authorization prompt.
OAuth tokens share the user's 5,000 requests per hour limit. GitHub App installation tokens scale with repos and users.
OAuth scopes are coarse: issues and pull requests need the full repo scope. GitHub Apps can request issues or pull requests without code access.
An OAuth App gets no notice when it loses access to an org or repo. Webhooks it created are not cleaned up when the token is deleted.
Orgs on Enterprise Cloud with SAML SSO: the user needs an active SSO session when authorizing, and must re-authorize after SSO is enabled.
Use state and PKCE (S256 only; plain is not supported). Re-check the user's identity with GET /user after every sign-in.
Revoking all permissions for an OAuth app deletes SSH keys (including deploy keys) the app created.

blockers.blocker: Org has OAuth app access restrictions on (default for new orgs), so the token cannot see private org repos
blockers.how_to_proceed: User clicks 'Request access' on the authorization page or in their app settings; an org owner approves under Third-party Access > OAuth app policy. Or switch to a GitHub App, which is installed per org and is not subject to OAuth app policies.

blockers.blocker: Users or security teams reject the broad repo scope
blockers.how_to_proceed: Build a GitHub App with fine-grained permissions and per-repository install, and bring its client ID and secret to Composio; send users the install link yourself.

blockers.blocker: Token store does not handle refresh tokens, and new apps expire tokens by default
blockers.how_to_proceed: Uncheck 'Expire user access tokens' until refresh is implemented, or let Composio manage the tokens.

blockers.blocker: SAML SSO org returns no data after connection
blockers.how_to_proceed: User opens https://github.com/orgs/ORG/sso to start an SSO session, then re-authorizes the app.

agent_can_do: Fill the registration form fields (name, homepage, description, callback URLs)
Generate the exact Composio redirect URI and callback URL list per environment
Choose a minimal OAuth scope list for the agent's tools, or a GitHub App permission set
Write the OAuth web flow with state and PKCE, and refresh-token rotation logic
Draft a customer help page on approving the app for an organization
Draft Marketplace listing copy and a privacy policy if a listing is wanted
Check that wildcard matching is off and that redirect URIs match exactly
you_must_do: Sign in to GitHub and create the app under the right owner (personal account or org)
Generate and store the client secret
Decide OAuth App vs GitHub App and the scope or permission set
Ask customer org owners to approve the app where restrictions apply
If listing paid plans on Marketplace: complete publisher verification and financial onboarding, and accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement
composio_note: Composio lists GitHub as 'Composio-managed OAuth available', so you can connect users with no app of your own; users will see Composio's app name on the consent screen. Bring your own OAuth App (custom auth config with client ID and secret, redirect URI https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add by default) to show your own name, request scopes beyond Composio's default 'repo,user,gist,notifications,project,workflow,codespace' (or fewer), get your own rate-limit quota instead of a shared one, or poll triggers more often than the 15-minute managed minimum. Composio also accepts a GitHub App's client ID and secret, but it does not send the app installation link; you give users that link yourself.

corrections: Common advice says GitHub OAuth App tokens never expire. Since 14 Aug 2026, new OAuth apps get expiring tokens (8h access, 6 month refresh) by default; older apps keep long-lived tokens unless they opt in. The 'Differences' page still says tokens are long-lived by default, which is out of date for new apps.
Common advice says an OAuth App can have only one callback URL. Since 14 Aug 2026 it can have up to 10.

Common advice says the redirect_uri may be any subpath of the callback URL. That is wildcard matching, now a per-URL setting; with it off, the match must be exact. Older single-callback apps have it on by default.
A privacy policy and logo are often listed as requirements; GitHub requires them only for a Marketplace listing, not for registration.
Evidence check 2026-10-28: one quoted scope list could not be found on the cited Composio page, so it was removed rather than kept as support.
